items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Stomata are tiny mouths that decide between starving and drying
items.claim: A leaf has hundreds of stomata per square millimetre. Open them: CO2 enters for photosynthesis but water evaporates away. Close them: water is saved but photosynthesis stalls. Plants must decide minute by minute.
items.prompt: How do guard cells open and close the stomatal pore?

options.text: Guard cells actively pump K+ ions in; water follows by osmosis; the cell swells; thicker inner walls force the cell to bow outward, opening the pore. Reverse the process to close

items.reveal:
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells. Their inner walls (facing the pore) are thicker and less elastic than their outer walls.

Opening: blue light activates a proton pump (H+-ATPase). The cells become more negative inside; K+ flows in via channels. Cl- and malate follow. Water enters by osmosis. Turgor rises. The thinner outer walls expand more than the inner walls, pulling the cells apart and opening the pore.

Closing: ABA (abscisic acid, the drought-stress hormone) triggers K+ efflux. The cells lose water and shrink. The pore closes.

Most plants close stomata at night (no photosynthesis needed) and during drought. CAM plants invert this. Wheat loses ~500 kg of water per kg of grain produced — most through stomata.

Climate change is forcing plants to evolve stomatal density: rising CO2 lets leaves get the same carbon with fewer stomata, reducing water loss.
items.why: Stomatal regulation is the central trade-off of land plant life. Engineering stomata for higher water-use efficiency is a major target of crop science.

items.title: Your lungs have the surface area of half a tennis court
items.claim: Two lungs, about 4 to 6 litres total volume — but the internal surface area where gas exchange happens is 50 to 75 square metres. Achieved by 300 to 500 million alveoli, each a tiny sphere with a thin shared wall to a capillary.
items.prompt: Why is so much surface area needed?

options.text: Diffusion of gases across a membrane scales with surface area and inversely with thickness; meeting the body's O2 demand (~250 ml/min at rest, ~3 L/min at exercise) requires both a huge area and an ultra-thin barrier (~0.5 micrometres)
Extra alveoli are spare in case some collapse

items.reveal:
Rate of diffusion = (surface area * concentration gradient) / (membrane thickness). To maximise O2 uptake, organisms maximise area, maximise gradient (high O2 in air vs low in blood) and minimise thickness.

Alveoli: 0.2-0.5 mm diameter spheres, lined with type I cells (extremely thin), surrounded by capillaries. The blood-air barrier is only 2-3 cells thick — sometimes <0.5 micrometres.

If you flattened all alveoli out, they would cover ~70 square metres — close to a singles tennis court.

Diseases that destroy alveoli (emphysema) reduce gas exchange capacity. Pulmonary fibrosis thickens the barrier. Both cause shortness of breath at exertion.

Total lung capillary blood volume is only ~75 ml at rest, but blood transits in ~0.75 seconds — enough for full equilibration in healthy lungs. At maximal exercise, transit time can drop to 0.25 seconds; in well-trained athletes at altitude, diffusion can become rate-limiting.
items.why: Big surface in small volume seems like a packaging miracle. Evolution solved it with tessellated bubbles — and made breathing possible at human body size.
